Answer ALL questions. For your guidance the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated in brackets. Mathematical formulae and tables, published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

The paper contains eight questions.

questions.corrige_markdown:
Simple harmonic motion means that the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite to it: $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -n^2 x$ with $n^2>0$, with no term in $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$.

Comparing with $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} + p\dfrac{dx}{dt} + qx = 0$, the resisting term must vanish and the restoring term must have the correct sign:

$$\boxed{\,p = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad q > 0\,}$$

The motion is then $x = A\cos(\sqrt q\,t) + B\sin(\sqrt q\,t)$, of constant amplitude and period $2\pi/\sqrt q$.
themes: simple harmonic motion of a particle

questions.corrige_markdown:
The auxiliary equation of $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} + p\dfrac{dx}{dt} + qx = 0$ is $m^2 + pm + q = 0$, with roots
$$m = \frac{-p \pm\sqrt{p^2-4q}}{2}.$$

Damped harmonic motion (decaying oscillations) requires **complex conjugate roots** with a **negative real part**:

- complex roots: $p^2 - 4q < 0$, i.e. $p^2 < 4q$ (this forces $q > 0$);
- real part $-\dfrac p2 < 0$ for a decay (a resisting medium), i.e. $p > 0$.

$$\boxed{\,p > 0 \quad\text{and}\quad p^2 < 4q\ \ (\text{equivalently } 0<p<2\sqrt q)\,}$$

(If $p^2 = 4q$ the damping is critical and if $p^2 > 4q$ it is heavy, so neither case oscillates; $p=0$ is the undamped case of part (i).)

questions.enonce_markdown: In the case where the motion is damped harmonic, find the damping factor. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
For $0<p<2\sqrt q$ the roots are $m = -\dfrac p2 \pm i\omega$ with
$$\omega = \frac{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}{2},$$
so the general solution is
$$x = e^{-pt/2}\,\big(A\cos\omega t + B\sin\omega t\big).$$

The oscillating bracket has constant amplitude, so the amplitude of the motion is multiplied by the factor $e^{-pt/2}$ as time goes on:

$$\boxed{\,\text{damping factor} = e^{-pt/2}\,}$$

i.e. the decay rate is $\dfrac p2$ (in the standard form $\ddot x + 2k\dot x + n^2x = 0$ this is $k = p/2$). Equivalently, successive maxima, one period $T$ apart, are in the constant ratio $e^{-pT/2} = \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi p}{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}\right)$.

questions.enonce_markdown: In the case where the motion is damped harmonic, find the period of the motion. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The motion $x = e^{-pt/2}(A\cos\omega t + B\sin\omega t)$ repeats its oscillation with angular frequency $\omega = \dfrac{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}{2}$, so the period is

$$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{\tfrac12\sqrt{4q-p^2}}$$

$$\boxed{\,T = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}\,}$$
